planting.note: Sow seed in fall, or set small rooted offsets, into a lean, sharply drained scree or tufa mix in full sun; keep the woolly crown elevated on grit through winter, since trapped moisture in the dense hairs rots the cushion faster than cold ever will.

directions: Hairy whitlow-grass forms one of the most densely woolly cushions among the rock garden Drabas, a hard silver-gray hummock built from countless minute rosettes packed so tightly that individual leaves are hard to distinguish. Native to the Caucasus, it produces disproportionately large sprays of bright yellow four-petaled flowers on very short stalks in spring, almost obscuring the cushion for a few weeks. Growth is glacially slow, so give it a permanent, uncrowded spot in a trough, raised scree, or tufa block with scrupulous drainage and a fresh grit top-dressing renewed each year. It is far more likely to be lost to a wet winter than a cold one, so overhead rain protection is worthwhile in humid climates.

planting.note: Sow seed in fall into a lean, sharply drained, limestone-grit scree or trough mix in full sun; this Pyrenean and Cantabrian endemic wants its roots run over broken rock rather than ordinary soil.

directions: Native to limestone crags of the Pyrenees and Cantabrian Mountains, this compact cushion Draba stands out from most of its yellow-flowered relatives by producing small pure white, four-petaled flowers held just above the tight mound of tiny hairy rosettes in spring. It forms a hard, slow-growing hummock well suited to a limestone scree bed, trough, or tufa block, where its neat gray-green cushion provides interest even out of bloom. As with other cushion Drabas, the greatest threat is winter wet rather than cold, so site it where rain drains away instantly and top-dress with fine limestone grit around the crown. Division of small rooted sections in spring is a reliable way to increase named or particularly compact forms.

planting.note: Sow seed in fall into a gritty, sharply drained scree or trough mix in full sun; native to the high mountains of Turkey and the Caucasus, it wants lean mineral soil rather than garden loam.

directions: This cushion-forming Draba from the mountains of Turkey and the Caucasus builds a dense mound of small, densely packed rosettes reminiscent of the unrelated shrub Brunia in overall texture, giving rise to its species name. In spring it is covered in clusters of small, mustard-yellow, four-petaled flowers held on short stalks just above the foliage. It shares the culture of other cushion alpine Drabas, demanding a lean, gritty, sharply drained scree, trough, or raised bed in full sun and resenting any prolonged winter moisture at the crown far more than cold temperatures. Top-dress with grit annually and avoid crowding by faster-growing neighbors, since growth is slow and the cushion can be smothered easily.

planting.note: Sow seed in fall, needing a cold winter to break dormancy, or plant rooted rosettes in spring into a gritty scree or trough mix in full sun; small individual rosettes should be spaced closely since the loose cushions build up gradually.

directions: Native to the Alps and Pyrenees, pink rock jasmine forms a loose cushion of small, narrow-leaved rosettes that in late spring produces short stalks each topped by a tight cluster of pink flowers with a contrasting yellow eye. It is a more approachable introduction to true cushion androsaces than some of the tightest Himalayan species, tolerating a standard scree or trough mix as long as drainage is sharp and the crown stays dry over winter. Grow it in full sun with excellent air movement to discourage the fungal rots that plague the genus in humid climates, and top-dress with grit to keep moisture off the foliage. Established cushions slowly increase in size and can be divided in spring if a piece is needed for a new planting.

planting.note: Sow seed in fall into a gritty, sharply drained scree or tufa mix in full sun; the densely hairy rosettes must stay dry in winter, so overhead glass or a steeply tilted crevice greatly improves survival outside an alpine house.

directions: This European alpine forms a tight, silvery cushion of densely hairy rosettes so covered in fine white hairs that the foliage appears almost felted, a texture that helps reflect intense high-altitude sun but also readily traps damaging moisture. In early summer the cushion is topped with small white to pale pink flowers with a yellow eye that deepens to red-orange as the bloom ages, giving a two-toned effect across the mound. It is one of the more demanding rock jasmines in cultivation and is best grown in an alpine house, raised tufa block, or a steeply angled crevice where winter rain sheds away instantly rather than sitting in the wool. Avoid overhead watering entirely once established and rely on the surrounding scree to wick moisture to the roots.

planting.note: Sow seed in fall and leave exposed to a full winter outdoors for reliable cold-stratified spring germination, into a gritty, humus-lean scree mix in full sun; this circumboreal species is among the more cold-hardy and garden-tolerant rock jasmines.

directions: Sweet-flowered rock jasmine has one of the widest natural ranges of any true alpine, occurring in a circumboreal band across the mountains of North America, Europe, and Asia, and is correspondingly one of the hardiest and most adaptable androsaces to grow. It forms a loose mat of small hairy rosettes that in late spring bear clusters of fragrant white flowers with a yellow eye that gradually flushes pink as the blooms age. Give it a gritty, sharply drained scree or rock garden site in full sun; it tolerates somewhat more routine garden conditions and cold than the tightest Himalayan cushion species, though winter wet at the crown should still be avoided. Established colonies spread gently by short stolons and can be divided in spring to start new plantings.

planting.note: Plant container-grown starts in fall or early spring into a gritty, sharply drained crevice or raised scree bed in full sun to light shade; this species tolerates somewhat more routine moisture than L. tweedyi but still needs excellent drainage at the crown.

directions: Columbia lewisia grows naturally on rocky cliffs and outcrops from the Columbia River Gorge north through the Cascades and Coast Ranges into British Columbia, forming evergreen rosettes of narrow, fleshy leaves. In early summer it sends up branching sprays of small pink flowers etched with darker rose veining, a more delicate and airy display than the larger-flowered Lewisia cotyledon. It is somewhat more forgiving of average rock garden moisture than several of its relatives but still performs best in a crevice or raised scree bed with sharp drainage and full sun to light afternoon shade in hot climates. Established plants resent root disturbance, so site them permanently and avoid moving mature rosettes once they take hold.

planting.note: Sow seed in fall for natural winter chilling, into a gritty, moisture-retentive-yet-fast-draining scree or trough mix in full sun; unlike the evergreen lewisias, this species needs some spring moisture during growth but then goes fully dormant and dry by midsummer.

directions: Nevada lewisia is a small, deciduous relative of the showier evergreen Lewisia species, native to rocky seeps, gravelly meadows, and snowmelt-fed slopes across the Sierra Nevada, Cascades, and northern Rockies. In late spring it produces simple, star-shaped white (occasionally pale pink) flowers held just above a low rosette of narrow succulent leaves, then dies back completely to a resting corm by midsummer as its native habitat dries out. Because it grows and flowers during the moist snowmelt period, give it more spring moisture than a typical Lewisia cotyledon, but keep it bone dry through summer dormancy in a gritty, fast-draining scree or trough. It is a subtle, easily overlooked plant best sited where its summer disappearance will not be mistaken for a dead planting.

planting.note: Sow seed in fall for natural winter chilling into a lean, gritty, high-alpine scree or trough mix in full sun; this dwarf species is extremely cold-hardy but resents rich soil or summer wet.

directions: Pygmy bitterroot is a diminutive, widespread high-elevation species found on gravelly alpine and subalpine slopes throughout the Rocky Mountains and Sierra Nevada, forming a tiny rosette of narrow succulent leaves that dies back after flowering in a manner similar to L. nevadensis. Its small flowers range from white to deep pink, often with darker veining, held on very short stems close to the ground where they are somewhat protected from wind at high altitude. Its natural habitat is thin, gritty, mineral soil with a long, cold, snow-covered winter, so it is best grown in a scree bed, trough, or crevice with sharp drainage and minimal organic matter, and it appreciates a site that mimics its native winter snow cover for reliable flowering. Because plants are small and easily lost among more vigorous neighbors, mark plantings clearly during summer dormancy.

planting.note: Plant container-grown starts in fall or early spring at a slight angle into an extremely well-drained, gritty crevice or trough in full sun; this narrow Sierra Nevada endemic tolerates a bit more summer moisture than L. tweedyi but still demands sharp drainage.

directions: Long-petaled lewisia is a rare, narrowly distributed species found only on high talus slopes near Lake Tahoe in the central Sierra Nevada, where snowmelt keeps its roots cool and moist while excellent drainage prevents standing water. It forms small, glossy evergreen rosettes similar to Lewisia cotyledon but more compact, topped from late spring into summer with bright pink flowers. Because it naturally receives more consistent moisture during the growing season than most evergreen lewisias, it is a valuable parent species behind many modern compact, floriferous garden hybrids sold under names like 'Little Plum' and 'Little Mango'. Grow it in a crevice or trough with sharp drainage and full sun, watering somewhat more generously in spring than other Lewisia species while still avoiding standing moisture at the crown.

common_name: Ashwood Strain Lewisia (English-Bred Siskiyou Lewisia Mix)

planting.note: Plant in spring at a slight angle into fast-draining, gritty soil in full sun, in a rock crevice, trough, or raised bed; being a seed-raised strain, expect variation in flower color from plant to plant.

directions: 'Ashwood Strain' is a seed strain of Siskiyou lewisia developed by the well-known English alpine nursery Ashwood Nurseries, selected over many generations for vigorous, well-branched flower sprays and an especially broad and clean color range spanning white, yellow, apricot, pink, and magenta. It shares the evergreen paddle-leaved rosette and general culture of the species, requiring a tilted crevice, trough, or raised scree bed with extremely sharp drainage to keep the crown from rotting in wet weather. Because it is grown from seed rather than propagated as a single clone, individual plants will vary somewhat in flower color and pattern, which is considered part of the strain's charm when planted in a group. Reduce watering once spring bloom finishes and the rosettes settle into their characteristic summer semi-dormancy.

planting.note: Sow seed in fall and leave exposed to natural winter cold for germination the following spring, into a gritty, mineral, sharply drained scree or trough mix in full sun to light shade; this circumpolar species needs consistently cool roots and struggles in hot summer climates.

directions: Purple mountain saxifrage is one of the hardiest flowering plants on Earth, growing farther north than almost any other species and blooming on Arctic tundra and high mountain scree from the moment snow releases its grip. It forms a tight, wiry mat of tiny opposite leaves that practically disappears beneath disproportionately large, stemless magenta-purple flowers in earliest spring, often the very first color in an alpine garden each year. It is far better suited to cool, northern, or high-elevation climates than to hot summer regions, where it struggles and often declines regardless of drainage; a north-facing scree, trough, or crevice with cool root conditions gives the best results. Keep the wiry mat gritty and lean, dividing congested patches occasionally to maintain vigor and prevent the center of the mat from dying out.

planting.note: Sow seed in fall or plant divisions in spring into a gritty, alkaline, sharply drained scree, wall crevice, or tufa mix in full sun to light shade; this is among the toughest and most garden-tolerant of the encrusted saxifrages.

directions: Livelong saxifrage belongs to the encrusted (silver) group of alpine saxifrages, forming rosettes of narrow, gray-green leaves rimmed with a fine crust of lime deposited from pores along the leaf margin, giving the foliage a distinctive silvered edge that persists year-round. In early summer, wiry, arching stems rise from the rosettes carrying open sprays of small, star-shaped white to pale cream flowers, after which the flowering rosette dies while offset rosettes carry the clump forward. It is one of the longest-lived and easiest true alpine saxifrages, tolerating an ordinary rock garden or wall-top position with sharp drainage far better than the tightest cushion species, and it thrives on alkaline, mineral soils. Remove spent flowering rosettes after bloom to tidy the clump and make room for the offsets already forming around them.

planting.note: Sow seed in fall into a gritty, alkaline scree or tufa mix, or plant rooted rosettes in a vertical crevice, in full sun to light shade; a near-vertical planting angle helps shed the winter moisture this cushion resents most.

directions: Native to limestone cliffs of the Maritime Alps, this encrusted saxifrage builds a dense silvery-gray hummock of small spoon-shaped rosettes, each leaf edged in a fine lime crust that catches the light and gives the whole cushion a frosted appearance. In late spring, airy, red-tinted stems rise well above the foliage carrying loose sprays of small white flowers, a striking contrast to the tight silver mound below. Like most encrusted saxifrages it grows best tucked into a vertical or steeply tilted limestone crevice, tufa block, or trough where rain runs off immediately rather than collecting around the crown. Give it full sun in cooler climates but afternoon shade where summers are hot, and top-dress with limestone chips to keep the cushion's silvering crisp.

planting.note: Start seed indoors in late winter or divide established mats in spring, planting into humus-rich, evenly moist but well-drained soil in partial shade; unlike the encrusted saxifrages, this mossy hybrid group prefers cooler, shadier sites with more consistent moisture.

directions: Mossy saxifrage is a garden hybrid group, not a wild species, developed largely from crosses among European Saxifraga species and prized for the dense, moss-like evergreen mats it forms rather than the tight mineral cushions of its cliff-dwelling relatives. In spring the mats disappear beneath a haze of small, five-petaled flowers in shades of white, pink, or red held on short wiry stems just above the foliage. Unlike sun-loving encrusted and Kabschia saxifrages, this hybrid group actually prefers a cooler, partly shaded site with humus-rich soil that stays evenly moist without becoming waterlogged, making it a good choice for the shadier side of a rock garden or a woodland-edge crevice. Divide congested mats every few years in spring or immediately after flowering to maintain vigor and refresh plantings.

common_name: Warley Rose Persian Stonecress (Compact Pink Rock Cress Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant cutting-grown starts in spring into lean, gritty, alkaline to neutral, sharply drained soil in full sun; propagate by softwood cuttings after flowering rather than seed, since this hybrid does not come true and can be short-lived.

directions: 'Warley Rose' is a classic, award-winning garden hybrid between two Mediterranean stonecress species, prized for its compact, blue-gray-leaved mound that is smothered from late spring into early summer in dense clusters of clear rose-pink, four-petaled flowers. It shares the heat- and drought-loving nature of its parent species, thriving in lean, gritty, sharply drained soil and actually performing better in a hot, dry summer than a cool, damp one. Because it is a hybrid clone, propagate it from softwood cuttings taken after flowering rather than seed, which will not reproduce the true color and habit. Plants are often relatively short-lived, especially in wet or rich soil, so keep a few rooted cuttings coming along to replace older, woodier mounds as they decline.

common_name: Dr Hanele Fairy Foxglove (Deep Carmine Alpine Erinus)

planting.note: Surface-sow fine seed in spring directly into gritty crevices of a dry stone wall, scree, or paving joint in full sun to partial shade; isolate from the plain species if you want seedlings to hold this darker color reliably.

directions: 'Dr Hanele' is a deeper-colored selection of fairy foxglove, bearing short spikes of small snapdragon-like flowers in an intense carmine-red rather than the more common magenta-pink of the wild species. It shares the same easy, self-sowing nature as the species, forming small semi-evergreen rosettes that colonize gritty wall crevices, gravel paths, and scree edges over a few seasons. Grow it in lean, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade exactly as you would the species, and expect some seedlings to revert toward paler pink over time unless it is grown in isolation from other Erinus. Shear off spent flower spikes to tidy the planting and moderate the volume of self-sown seedlings.

planting.note: Surface-sow fine seed in spring directly into gritty crevices of a dry stone wall, scree, or paving joint in full sun to partial shade; grow away from pink-flowered Erinus if you want self-sown seedlings to stay reliably white.

directions: 'Albus' is a pure white-flowered selection of fairy foxglove, giving the same short spikes of small tubular flowers as the species but in crisp white rather than the typical pink to magenta, making it a useful cooling contrast when planted alongside the species in wall crevices or gravel paths. It grows and self-sows just as readily as the wild form, forming small semi-evergreen rosettes that spread themselves into new cracks and gaps over time. Culture is identical to the species: lean, gritty, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, with little care needed beyond an occasional shearing of spent flower spikes. Because Erinus crosses and self-sows freely, keep it away from pink-flowered forms if you want the white color to remain dominant in future seedlings.

planting.note: Divide established clumps or set out nursery starts in spring into ordinary, well-drained garden soil in full sun; division is far more reliable than seed, which needs cold stratification and germinates slowly and unevenly.

directions: Southern globe daisy is a taller, more upright relative of the mat-forming rock garden Globularia species, growing as a clump of leathery basal leaves topped by wiry stems bearing powder-blue, pincushion-like flowerheads in late spring. Unlike the cushion-forming Globularia cordifolia, it does not spread as a creeping mat, making it better suited to the front of a border or a raised bed edge than a crevice or trough. It grows easily in ordinary, well-drained garden soil in full sun and needs little care beyond removing spent flower stems, tolerating both heat and modest drought once established. Divide clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor and to generate new plants for other parts of the garden.

planting.note: Divide established rosettes or set out nursery starts in spring into a gritty, alkaline, sharply drained scree mix in full sun; seed needs cold stratification and germinates slowly, so division is more dependable.

directions: Native to limestone screes of the Pyrenees and Alps, this compact Globularia forms a low rosette of leathery, dark green leaves from which entirely leafless, wiry stalks rise a few inches to carry rounded, powder-blue flowerheads in late spring, a habit that gives the species its name. It is a genuine limestone specialist, growing best in a gritty, sharply drained scree bed or trough with an alkaline to neutral mineral mix rather than average garden soil. Full sun and excellent drainage keep the rosettes tight and encourage the best flowering, while heavy or wet soils quickly lead to rot. Established clumps increase slowly and can be divided in spring if additional plants are wanted, though disturbance is best kept to a minimum.

planting.note: Sow seed in fall into a gritty, alkaline scree or vertical tufa crevice, or set young pot-grown plants into a sheltered limestone crack in partial shade; this notoriously fussy Dolomites endemic wants its long taproot run deep into cool, mineral rock rather than open soil.

directions: Devil's claw is one of the most sought-after and challenging true alpines in cultivation, a limestone-cliff endemic of the southern Alps and Dolomites that produces one of the botanical world's strangest flowers: a tight, bristling tuft of pale lilac-to-purple, bottle-shaped blooms with narrow, curved beaks that genuinely resemble tiny claws or horns. It grows a long taproot deep into rock crevices in the wild, so cultivation almost always means a vertical tufa block or a deep, narrow crack packed with a gritty, alkaline mix rather than an open scree bed. Give it light shade in hot climates and cool, constantly available moisture at depth combined with a bone-dry surface, since both drought at the root and standing wet at the crown are fatal. Most growers treat any specimen that survives more than a couple of seasons as a considerable success, and propagation is almost always from fresh seed rather than division.

planting.note: Sow seed in spring into a gritty, sharply drained scree or trough mix in full sun; this Balkan native resents winter wet more than cold and benefits from a grit top-dressing around the crown.

directions: Grassy bells forms a low tuft of narrow, grass-like silvery leaves native to rocky slopes across the Balkan Peninsula, closely related to Campanula but distinguished by its clustered, upward-facing bell flowers rather than the typical nodding campanula bloom. In early summer, dense heads of violet-blue, star-shaped bells open at the tips of short stems held just above the foliage tuft, lasting several weeks in cool weather. It needs the same sharp drainage and full sun as other true rock garden alpines, growing best in a scree bed, trough, or wall crevice with a gritty, lean mix, and it is markedly more tolerant of heat than many high-alpine cushion plants. Deadhead spent flower heads to prolong bloom and prevent the tuft from expending energy on unwanted self-sown seedlings.

planting.note: Sow seed in fall into a lean, sharply drained scree or tufa mix in full sun; this Dalmatian coast endemic forms an extremely tight cushion and needs scrupulous drainage to avoid winter rot.

directions: Dwarf grassy bells is a compact, cushion-forming relative of the taller Edraianthus graminifolius, endemic to limestone mountains along the Dalmatian coast, where it forms a dense silvery hummock of narrow, hair-fine leaves. In early summer the tiny cushion produces disproportionately large, upward-facing lavender-blue bells that sit almost directly on the foliage with barely any visible stem, a striking contrast of scale that makes it a prized trough and tufa subject. It demands the sharpest possible drainage, growing best in a raised scree bed, trough, or tufa block with a lean, gritty mix and a fresh grit top-dressing around the crown each year. Like most extreme cushion alpines, it is more likely to be lost to winter wet than winter cold, so overhead rain protection is worthwhile in humid climates.
